notes.subject: plate
notes.text: Long white plates with blue strips on both sides, the left one more visible; some older ones lack the right strip and have a yellow rear plate.

notes.subject: bollard
notes.text: Extremely common round white bollard with a pointed top and a grey or red reflector band all the way around.

notes.subject: bollard
notes.text: A round white bollard with two indented reflective bands is unique here; green and yellow versions exist, and wedge-shaped ones with wide rectangular reflectors too.

notes.subject: pole
notes.text: Concrete poles with step-like indents, called ladder or waffle poles, plus wooden and thin octagonal metal poles in rural areas.

notes.subject: pole
notes.text: Small blue rectangular plates on utility poles are unique here, found on almost all wooden and metal poles.

notes.subject: pole
notes.text: Diamond-shaped pole tops with three wires, mostly on ladder poles; arrowhead-like variants with insulators on top are unique here.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Small yellow signs showing a road number starting with D, on top of direction or town entry signs, are unique here.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Direction signs are white with an arrow-shaped black outline offset from the edge, thickening at the point; small places often use italics.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Road and town entry signs have a red border with a thin white outline, often with a white text plate below; the neighbour to the south has a thick red border to the edge.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Flat rectangular signposts, often very short, sometimes dyed unusual colours; shared only with a few southwestern neighbours.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Chevrons are white arrows on blue, with one to five arrows; the southern neighbour only has two or four.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Pedestrian signs have five stripes and a disconnected head; a two-dashed-line design is rarer.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Kilometre markers usually show a yellow or red semicircle atop a white rectangle, as a waystone or flat sign.

notes.subject: line
notes.text: Middle dashes made of two offset blocks are unique here, so you can safely guess this country; unusually long dashes are also a clue.

notes.subject: line
notes.text: Arrows marking the end of a passing zone appear, with middle dashes very close together.

notes.subject: guardrail
notes.text: Mostly A-type guardrails without reflectors; thin B-type occasionally appears in the north.

notes.subject: other
notes.text: Tall rectangles on sticks in the colours of the Austrian flag line some roads and are found nowhere else.

notes.subject: language
notes.text: A Romance language with é, à, è, ù, â, ê, ç, œ and the -ux ending; the word for street is rue.

notes.subject: architecture
notes.text: Mostly stone houses, unpainted or in grey or yellow pastels, simple gable roofs with orange tiles or black slate, townhouses wall to wall.

notes.subject: other
notes.text: House numbers are most commonly blue, in a serif font; the southeastern neighbour almost never uses blue ones.

notes.subject: car
notes.text: Peugeot, Renault and Citroën make up almost half of all cars.

notes.subject: other
notes.text: Includes smallcam coverage; on rare generation 3 you may see a coloured flag on the antenna, unique here.

notes.subject: other
notes.text: Phone numbers have 10 digits; 01 is the capital region and 02 to 05 go clockwise from the northwest; 06 to 09 are not regional.

notes.subject: other
notes.text: Five-digit postal codes start with the two-digit department number, the same code shown in the plate's right strip.

notes.subject: other
notes.text: Most departments have their own logo on bus stops, markers and direction signs; the southern region has a red and yellow cross flag.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: Roads with a red or purple tint are most common between the capital and Dijon, apart from Normandy.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Dark green signposts and backs are common in Brittany, around the capital and in several southern regions.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: A dark green post with a lighter green or turquoise signback, sometimes with a green and blue triangle logo, marks Pas-de-Calais.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Signs with brown posts and backs are most common in Seine-et-Marne.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Most town entry signs in Marne are one thick combined block for entry and exit.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Green sticker logos on signbacks and D-roads with decimal numbers are most common in Eure-et-Loir.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Direction signs in Haute-Garonne often use burgundy attachments, sometimes with yellow posts.

notes.subject: other
notes.text: Cuboid stone-and-mortar barriers are common on Corsica; rounded-top ones are not.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: Rural roads enclosed by view-blocking hedges, like the British Isles, are most common in the northwest, especially Normandy.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: Stone pines line the southern coast; fully maritime pine forests on flat ground are in the southwest, Gironde and Landes.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: Sunflowers are mostly in the southwest, particularly around Toulouse.

notes.subject: architecture
notes.text: Black shingle roofs are mostly northwest of the Loire, and also near the northern border, the south-centre and the Pyrenees.

notes.subject: architecture
notes.text: Brittany has black roofs, edge chimneys, black slate walls and stone surrounds around doors and windows.

notes.subject: architecture
notes.text: Southern roofs use rounded overlapping tiles in varying colours.

notes.subject: architecture
notes.text: Rows of dark red brick houses with white mortar lines near the northern border resemble Flemish style.

notes.subject: architecture
notes.text: Bright orange brick buildings with wooden shutters fill old towns in and around Toulouse.

notes.subject: architecture
notes.text: The Riviera has palms, light multi-storey buildings with wide balconies and blue-painted signposts, like its tiny coastal neighbour.

notes.subject: architecture
notes.text: White houses with colourful timber framing in matching shutters and gates are Basque in style.

notes.subject: architecture
notes.text: Timber framing, half-hip roofs and fish-scale tiles are concentrated in the east.

notes.subject: language
notes.text: A Celtic language with ñ, k and w appears on bilingual signs across Brittany, as far east as Rennes; Plou- town names are in the northwest.

notes.subject: language
notes.text: Bilingual signs in an isolate language with K, X and Z appear in the western half of the southwestern department; street is karrika.

notes.subject: language
notes.text: Southern signs may show Occitan (carrièra, carriero) or, in the far south, a language where street is carrer.

notes.subject: language
notes.text: Corsican signs on the island end in vowels, with u, iu or ju endings and Italian-style place names.

notes.subject: other
notes.text: River-based names use -sur- plus a river; names with -sur-mer or -plage are exclusively coastal.

notes.subject: architecture
notes.text: Steep black mansard roofs with dormer windows are very common in the capital.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: Lavender fields appear in the southeast.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: Salt farms like flooded trenches with grass medians line the Atlantic coast, around Guérande, Noirmoutier, Île de Ré and Oléron.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: The capital's street signs are green and Prussian blue with a top arch; Lyon's have four corner bolts; Marseille's show the city emblem.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Street signs with a red slanted fleur-de-lis are unique to Lille.

notes.subject: guardrail
notes.text: Thin B-type guardrails appear on highways in the northern half, around Le Mans, Tours, the capital, Reims and Metz.
